newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel starts work on Jerusalem settlement.
newsitem.headline: Israel starts work on Jerusalem settlement.

text.p: Israel broke ground on Tuesday for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, defying world opinion and vowing not to flinch from a showdown with Palestinians.

"It is a black day for the peace process," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters in Gaza. He said President Yasser Arafat would summon the Palestinian leadership later in the day to decide on a response to the project.

Faisal al-Husseini, the senior PLO official in Jerusalem, said at a protest tent-camp opposite the Jabal Abu Ghneim site that the groundbreaking left Palestinians with only one option -- "to go down to the streets".
In Amman, the Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas, which opposes the 1993 peace deal between the PLO and Israel, called for a Palestinian uprising to protest the start of work.
"The Palestinian Authority should answer the call of the Palestinian people to go into continuous intifada (uprising)," Hamas spokesman Ibrahim Ghoshe told Reuters.
Surveyors set up tripods on the pine-covered hill, which Israel calls Har Homa, and one of four bulldozers that arrived in a heavily guarded convoy began digging immediately.
"Roads are the first stage," contractor Sasson Shem-Tov, overseeing the work, told Reuters.

Israeli troops ringed the hill and security sources said snipers and tanks were put on alert to move into trouble spots. Witnesses said at least three Israeli Arab students who tried to reach the protest camp were beaten by soldiers.
Police chiefs decided to rush hundreds of reinforcements to Jerusalem in anticipation of a violent Palestinian backlash.
"We will not get down on our knees," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said.
Arafat told reporters in Gaza he had urged his people not to resort to violence. "I have done it," he said, when asked if he had issued the appeal.
Netanyahu's government intends to build 6,500 homes for Jews at the site, called Har Homa by Israel.
The settlement will be another link in a concrete chain of apartment blocks that Israel has built to cement its hold on East Jerusalem and separate it from the rest of the West Bank.
But the internationally condemned project threatened to crack the foundations of a shaky Middle East peace process. U.N. observers were at the site.
National police chief Assaf Hefetz said police were preparing "for the ground to get hot".
Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani warned the Palestinian Authority not to opt for violence over what it views as a violation of the Israel-PLO peace deals.
"If it lets trigger-happy people act...it will simply be making a very grave mistake. We are prepared for any flareup. Our reaction will be sharp, severe and strong," Kahalani said.
The Palestinian Health Ministry declared a state of emergency at hospitals in self-ruled parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, an official at Ramallah hospital said.
There seemed to be little chance of a summit between Netanyahu and Arafat which PLO officials said was conditioned on suspending the project.
Arafat spurned Netanyahu's appeals to meet him late on Monday, drawing Israeli accusations the Palestinian leader was trying to stoke already high tensions.
Dozens of Israeli soldiers in combat gear took up positions around the base of the hill as helicopters flew overhead.
"We are trying to do only one thing -- to have talks. If the Palestinian side is looking for a dialogue, we are also looking for one and not for confrontation," Naveh told Army Radio.
"But if the Palestinian side wants confrontation, we are also prepared for that," he said.
Israel said on Monday it had reinforced its troops in the West Bank and Gaza Strip to pre-empt any Palestinian violence.
The PLO wants East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war, as the capital of a Palestinian state. Israel regards all of Jerusalem as its "eternal capital".
Last September, 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in clashes that erupted after Netanyahu punched another opening into an archaeological tunnel in East Jerusalem.

Under the 1993 PLO-Israel peace accord, the future of Jerusalem and the fate of Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza will be determined in "final status" talks that were supposed to have resumed on Monday and end in 1999.

The settlement was approved under Israel's previous Labour-led government, an advocate of trading land for peace. Labour protests over Netanyahu's plans are muted by what politicians say is public consensus to retain all of Jerusalem.
